newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Diana, proud of new charity role, vows to press on.
newsitem.headline: Diana, proud of new charity role, vows to press on.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana, ending a trip to Angola on Thursday, said she had found new fulfilment as a champion of the fight to ban landmines, a crusade she now hopes to take to troublespots around the globe.
She brushed off criticism by politicians back home that she should mind her own business and not get involved in politics as "merely a distraction" and vowed not to change course.

"I am not a political figure, the fact is I am a humanitarian figure and always will be," the princess told reporters on the last day of her four-day trip to war-scarred Angola to highlight the misery landmines cause.

"This visit has given me the opportunity to experience at first hand the suffering caused by landmines," she said after meeting some of Angola's legion of amputees, victims of mines that still pepper the countryside three years into peace.
"It has convinced me I must continue to play a part in the ongoing worldwide campaign to ban landmines."
She nodded when asked if she wanted to visit Afghanistan, Bosnia and Cambodia to highlight the anti-mine campaign that she publicised in Angola on behalf of the British Red Cross.
A prominent member of British Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives rounded on Diana, who last year divorced heir to the throne Prince Charles, for being "very uninformed".
"This is an important, sophisticated argument. It doesn't help simply to point at the amputees and say how terrible it is," said Peter Viggers, of parliament's defence committee.
Since her bitter marital collapse left her on the outside of Britain's royal establishment, Diana has sought a new public role for herself.
Now, she seems to have found it with her trip to Angola.
"It is the type of format I have been looking for, for some time. I have had more contact with people and there has been less formality," she said. "It has been an intensive four days."

The 35-year-old mother of two princes stressed the visit's informality by paring down a usually hefty entourage to just one manservant, and by dressing down to show she meant work -- raising comparisons with Charles' hardworking sister, Anne.

During her Angola trip the glamorous princess, one of the world's most photographed women who hopes her fame has drawn attention to the cause, visited an artificial limb factory and chatted to children and adults maimed by landmines.
She detonated a mine in the dirt-poor countryside, where nine million mines -- one for every Angolan -- lie in wait, and was even presented with a defused anti-personnel mine as a gift.
Angola, recovering from a disastrous 20-year civil war, has the world's highest amputee rate at three per thousand people.
Diana, wearing jeans, a denim shirt and navy blazer, headed to Luanda airport on Thursday to return to London on scheduled flights via Johannesburg.
